title: Exposing Agents as MCP servers with mcp-agent: Sarmad Qadri
talk_summary: Sarmad Qadri argues MCP standardizes tool/agent interfaces and that agents should be exposed as MCP servers and run as durable async workflows. He demos mcp-agent with Temporal, an orchestrator plus specialist agents, and MCP-client invocation of a long-running workflow.

takeaways.what_they_do: Model each agent run as a workflow with persisted state, retries, pause/resume, and human-in-loop waits, using Temporal as durable execution backend.
takeaways.evidence_quote: agents are async workflows and they should be modeled as such because they can be paused, resumed, retried.

takeaways.what_they_do: Expose specialist agents as MCP servers so any MCP client or other agent can invoke them over the same protocol as tools.
takeaways.evidence_quote: agents should be thought of as uh microservices and they can be deployed as MCP servers themselves.

takeaways.what_they_do: Run agent workflows on dedicated infrastructure and let clients poll status/results, decoupling execution from the invoking chat/client.
takeaways.evidence_quote: where the agent compute is happening from uh the client that is being used to invoke the agent

takeaways.what_they_do: Pair a generator agent with an evaluator agent that scores output and feeds critiques back over iterations until quality bar is met.
takeaways.evidence_quote: evaluates the quality of the generated response and gives feedback to the to the generator LLM

takeaways.what_they_do: Dispatch independent subtasks to multiple subagents in parallel and aggregate their results before responding.
takeaways.evidence_quote: fanning out to multiple uh sub agents and then fanning back in uh to aggregate the results.

takeaways.what_they_do: Treat agents as workflows triggered by webhooks, cron, or human events rather than only chat sessions.
takeaways.evidence_quote: You could have a web hook that triggers an agent or a cron job
